Physical Intelligence in Smart Manufacturing.\", \"abstract\": \"Manufacturing is evolving from automation-centered production toward systems capable of sensing, adaptation, and autonomous response across digital, mechanical, and material domains. Although recent progress has been largely driven by artificial intelligence, current manufacturing intelligence often remains external to physical systems and suffers from limited robustness, interpretability, and transferability in complex industrial environments. Here, we present a unified perspective on smart manufacturing through the framework of artificial intelligence (AI), embodied intelligence (EI), and physical intelligence (PI). AI provides abstraction, prediction, and generative capability; EI enables closed-loop perception, decision-making, and physical interaction; and PI embeds adaptive intelligence directly into materials, structures, and physicochemical processes. We further discuss how generative intelligence is beginning to connect these domains through inverse design, adaptive fabrication, and physics-constrained behavior realization. Recent advances in collaborative robotics, embodied digital twins, self-optimizing production systems, and physically intelligent materials, including self-actuating, self-healing, multistable, and shape-morphing systems, are reviewed. Finally, we propose an integrated AI-EI-PI framework spanning the full manufacturing lifecycle, highlighting a transition toward manufacturing systems in which intelligence is increasingly co-designed across algorithms, embodied agents, and matter itself.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78384\", \"pmid\": \"42932218\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13703982\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78384\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13703982\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13703982?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"An Integrated Artificial Intelligence Framework for Nanomedicine Engineering.\", \"abstract\": \"The translation of nanomedicines is frequently bottlenecked by trial-and-error optimization. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) transforms this process into a closed-loop, experimentally grounded discovery ecosystem. This Review provides a roadmap for this paradigm, demonstrating how AI, high-throughput testing, and nanoscale design converge to generate clinically translatable nanotherapeutics. We emphasize the necessity of standardized multimodal data-spanning pharmacokinetic, biodistribution, and drug-release profiles-anchored strictly to validated biological phenomena. Furthermore, we evaluate an algorithmic spectrum, ranging from classical machine learning to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), to align models with specific formulation objectives. To bridge computational design and empirical reality, we examine how high-throughput technologies, such as robotic laboratories and in vivo DNA-barcoding multiplexing, operationalize the \\\"Design-Make-Test-Analyze\\\" (DMTA) cycle for dynamic model recalibration. Ultimately, this review demonstrates how integrating AI, physical constraints, and automated validation accelerates the rational design of next-generation nanomedicines.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78125\", \"pmid\": \"42934944\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13710834\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78125\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710834\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710834?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "f20711827e6c7566bed0db688005ca6de387dccc5907517d6c2fbdc31c4415e8", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1002/advs.78384", "doi:10.1002/advs.78125", "pmc:PMC13657930", "pmc:PMC13650560", "pmc:PMC13703982", "pmc:PMC13710834"], "source_candidates": ["https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13657930/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13657930/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13657930", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13657930?pdf=render", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13650560/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13650560/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13650560", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13650560?pdf=render"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
